svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "Hershey and Chase (1952): is the genetic material protein or DNA?"], [1, "Two batches of T2 phage: protein coats labelled with \u00b3\u2075S, or DNA labelled with \u00b3\u00b2P."], [3, "The phages infect E. coli and inject their genetic material into the cells."], [6.5, "A blender shakes the phage coats off the bacteria."], [9, "A centrifuge spins the bacteria into a pellet; coats stay in the supernatant."], [11.5, "Measure the radioactivity: \u00b3\u2075S in the supernatant, \u00b3\u00b2P in the pellet."], [13.5, "DNA entered the bacteria: DNA is the genetic material."]]
svg.title: The Hershey–Chase experiment
svg.desc: Two batches of T2 bacteriophage, one with sulfur-35 labelled protein and one with phosphorus-32 labelled DNA, infect E. coli; blending and centrifuging show that phosphorus-32, the DNA, ends up inside the bacteria.
svg.text: Radioactive label shown glowing. T2 phage infecting Escherichia coli.

g.data-info: Phages grown with radioactive sulfur-35. Sulfur is in proteins (cysteine and methionine) but not in DNA, so only the protein coat is labelled.
The phages attach to E. coli and inject their genetic material.
Shaking in a kitchen blender knocks the empty phage coats off the outside of the bacteria.
Spinning makes the heavier bacteria form a pellet at the bottom; the light phage coats stay in the liquid (supernatant).
³⁵S was mostly in the supernatant, ³²P mostly in the pellet with the bacteria. So DNA, not protein, enters the cell to make new phages: DNA is the genetic material.
Phages grown with radioactive phosphorus-32. Phosphorus is in the DNA backbone; proteins have very little, so the DNA is labelled.

g.text: P in DNA, little in protein
Conclusion: DNA, not protein, enters the bacteria → DNA is the genetic material
